name: The Bar That Passes At Four Feet And Fails At Forty
symptom: An exterior bar is present, bonded, in a reasonable width, and the window photographs well from the driveway. From across the street the grid dissolves and the sash reads as one sheet of glass with faint lines drawn on it. The bar is flat-faced or has a shallow single-radius edge, sits proud of the glass by 1/8 in or less, and is the same colour as the sash.

cause.explanation: An extruded or moulded bar is drawn as a shape in section, and a shape that has to be pulled from a die or a mould wants shallow relief and generous radii. A joiner's muntin is not a shape but an assembly: a moulded bar with the glass rebated 3/8 in behind its outer face and bedded in putty that is then struck to a bevel. The die cannot produce the rebate, so the manufacturer produces the width and drops the depth, on the reasonable assumption that width is what the customer specifies.
cause.cost_saved: The whole difference between a bonded flat bar at 25 to 60 USD a unit and a true or fully simulated assembly at 150 to 500 USD a unit.

rule_violated.statement: The sash section is 1 3/8 in deep and the muntin is 7/8 in wide; the projection dimension is the one that survives distance.

rule_violated.ref: beyond about thirty feet the eye stops resolving the width of a thin member and reads only its tonal contrast
rule_violated.statement: At 40 ft a 7/8 in bar subtends roughly 0.1 degrees, close to the limit of comfortable resolution. What remains legible is not the bar but the three-value sequence it generates — lit bevel, cast shadow, glass — and that sequence requires physical depth. A flat bar generates one value and vanishes.

correct_practice: Specify the muntin by section and setback, not only by width. Historic Anglo-American muntin: 7/8 in wide, moulded to an ovolo or ogee, glass rebated so the outer face of the bar stands 3/8 to 1/2 in in front of the glass surface, putty struck at about 30 degrees. Federal work runs the bar down toward 5/8 to 7/8 in and depends even more on the moulding, because there is less width to work with. The bar must also be a different tonal value from the sash where possible — historically the whole sash was one colour, but the depth supplied the difference, so a flat bar in the same colour as a flat sash has neither depth nor contrast.

fixes.right: True divided lights, or a simulated assembly with a moulded exterior bar standing 3/8 in proud of the glass and a matched shadow bar in the airspace.
fixes.cheap: Two moves at no material cost. First, take the widest bar the manufacturer offers rather than the narrowest — 1 1/8 in rather than 5/8 in — because on an assembly that has already lost its depth, width is the only remaining variable that carries at distance. Second, reduce the light count: a 6/6 sash with four fewer bars, each of them wider, reads far better at forty feet than a 12/12 with hairlines. This is the substitution the period itself made when glass got cheaper.
fixes.dishonest: Painting the bars a contrasting colour to make them show. It reads as a graphic applied to glass, which is exactly what it is, and it draws attention to the flatness rather than compensating for it.

detection: The forty-foot test is literal: photograph or view the elevation from the far kerb. If the grid is legible from the driveway and gone from the far side of the street, the bar has width and no depth. In a close photograph, look for the shadow — a bar with 3/8 in of setback casts a hard dark line onto the glass on its shaded side, roughly a third of the bar's own width, which is present in every photograph of an original sash and absent in almost every photograph of a modern one. Also check the bar's outer face for a moulded profile: a single flat plane with two small radii is an extrusion, an ovolo with a quirk is joinery.

exceptions.why: Federal sash is deliberately thin — muntins under 7/8 in and often nearer 5/8 in — and the style's whole late-Georgian refinement depends on the glazing bar being as slight as it can be made. A wide bar collapses the style at any distance beyond fifty feet.
exceptions.bounds: Thin, but moulded and rebated. The Federal licence is on width, never on depth: a 5/8 in bar with a proper ovolo and a 3/8 in setback is Federal, a 5/8 in flat applied bar is this fault. Federal glass is also larger than Georgian, so the thin bar comes with fewer lights, not more.

bounds_test.note: The Federal licence is on WIDTH only. 5/8 to 7/8 in, with a full ovolo and a 3/8 in setback. A 5/8 in flat applied bar scores inside the width bound and still fails the setback test, which is where the licence stops.

exceptions.why: Glazing bars of 12 to 18 mm, thinner than anything before, are the Regency signature and are what makes the window read as a sheet of light.
exceptions.bounds: Same bound as Federal: thin section, full moulding, real setback. Regency bars are often gunmetal or brass-reinforced precisely so they can be thin and still be moulded.

bounds_test.note: 12 to 18 mm, that is 0.47 to 0.71 in. Regency bars are often gunmetal or brass-reinforced precisely so they can be this thin and still be moulded.

exceptions.why: Craftsman muntins are wide and flat-faced by intent — not less than 1 1/8 in — because the idiom's whole language is broad flat members with square arrises.
exceptions.bounds: Width not less than 1 1/8 in, vertical bars only, upper sash only. The flatness is licensed; the absence of setback is not, and a Craftsman bar still stands proud of the glass.

bounds_test.note: The style's own floor, and the licence runs the other way: not less than 1 1/8 in, vertical bars, upper sash only.

granted_when.note: Applies to the upper sash only; the lower sash is a single light and has no bar to licence.

confused_with.difference: That fault is about a bar being too wide for the period. This one is about a bar of any width having no depth. A window can be too wide and too flat simultaneously, and most are.
That one has no exterior bar at all.

Same profile-depth mechanism at a different element. That fault is about carved ornament executed at the wrong depth for its period; this is about a glazing bar with width and no section. They share a cause and travel together on the same elevation.

sources: Period sash and glazier's price lists, crown and cylinder glass sizes
Marvin SDL bar width range 5/8, 7/8, 1 1/8, 1 15/16, 2 13/32 in

test.note: The dimension that survives distance. A putty-glazed muntin sets the glass 3/8 to 1/2 in behind the outer face of the bar, producing three tonal values at every joint — lit bevel, cast shadow, glass. An extruded or moulded bar sits 1/8 in proud or less and produces one. Read from the shadow band width in raking light rather than measured directly.

secondary_tests.note: The setback expressed as what a camera actually sees. Present in almost every photograph of an original sash and absent in almost every photograph of a modern one.

THE FORTY-FOOT TEST, stated as a test. Photograph the same window from the driveway and from the far kerb. A bar with depth scores 1; a bar with width and no depth scores 0. At 40 ft a 7/8 in bar subtends about 0.1 degrees, at the edge of comfortable resolution, so what remains legible is the three-value sequence and not the bar.

severity_by_style.why: The style's constraint says it directly: at fifty feet Federal versus Georgian is a muntin-width and cornice-depth judgement, and a bar with no shadow removes the evidence.
The thin bar is what makes a Regency window read as a sheet of light; with no moulding and no setback it reads as a sheet of glass with lines on it, which is the opposite effect.
Broad flat members with square arrises are the idiom's whole language, so flatness of face costs little here — but the bar still stands proud of the glass and the setback is not licensed.
An idiom that refuses casing and moulded sills is not going to be undone by a shallow glazing bar.
No claim is being made to pre-industrial joinery.

inverted_by.statement: Here a thin bar is the fault. The style's constraint sets a floor of 1 1/8 in and runs the bars vertically in the upper sash only; a 5/8 in bar in an equal grid is the Craftsman version of this error.
A slight bar is the fault. The bar is a compositional line and its weight is the point, so under-weighting it dissolves the geometry the window exists to draw.
